## Copilot prompt used to generate the analysis

I asked Copilot to help me write a compact R `dplyr` workflow that reads the NHANES CSV, drops rows with missing `BMI`, `IncomeGroup`, and `Gender`, groups by `IncomeGroup` and `Gender`, computes `n`, `mean_bmi`, and `sd_bmi`, and confirms the output matches the same analytic question as a Python/pandas translation. I also asked it to refactor the repeated logic into a reusable function so the value and grouping columns could be changed later without changing the structure of the analysis.

> Prompt to Copilot: "Using the NHANES case-study CSV in `examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv`, write an R `dplyr` pipeline that drops rows with missing BMI, IncomeGroup, and Gender, groups by IncomeGroup and Gender, calculates n, mean_bmi, and sd_bmi, and arranges the output by IncomeGroup and Gender. Then refactor this into a small reusable function that can summarize any numeric value by any two grouping columns while preserving the same missing-data rules and output structure. Keep the code reproducible and ready to compare against a pandas translation."

## Verification

I verified the generated code by running the pipeline and function in R, then checking that the filtered row count, grouped-row count, and summary values matched the same logic implemented in Python. The final parity audit confirms the row counts and rounded summary values are consistent across languages.

## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
nhanes <- read_csv("examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv")
```

## Part A: R pipeline

```{r}
r_summary <- nhanes |>
  filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bmi = round(mean(BMI), 2),
    sd_bmi = round(sd(BMI), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(IncomeGroup, Gender)

r_summary
```

## Part B: Reusable R function

```{r}
summarise_mean_sd <- function(data, value, group1, group2) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ value }}), !is.na({{ group1 }}), !is.na({{ group2 }})) |>
    group_by({{ group1 }}, {{ group2 }}) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_value = round(mean({{ value }}), 2),
      sd_value = round(sd({{ value }}), 2),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange({{ group1 }}, {{ group2 }})
}

r_function_summary <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, BMI, IncomeGroup, Gender)
r_function_summary
```

The function output has the same grouping structure as the original pipeline. I checked that the row count and group labels match before translating to Python.

### More R mastery exercises

#### Exercise 1: swap the value variable

```{r}
waist_summary <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, Waist, IncomeGroup, Gender)
waist_summary
```

This summary still uses the same six income-by-gender groups, but the row count is unchanged because the filter and grouping variables remain the same; only the measured variable changes.

#### Exercise 2: swap a grouping variable

```{r}
race_summary <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, BMI, Race, Gender)

race_summary
```

This summary has more rows because `Race` introduces additional categories beyond the three income bands. The total number of groups increases as a result.

## AI audit prompt

> Translate this R `dplyr` pipeline into Python/pandas one step at a time. For each step, explain the equivalent Python operation, the output I should inspect, and the parity check I should run against my R result. Do not combine steps or add new analysis choices.

## Python translation

The Python translation is saved in `translation.ipynb` in the same folder. It uses a small helper module, `helpers.py`, to keep the logic clean and reusable.

## Parity audit

The parity checks below compare the R and Python outputs for row counts, missingness handling, grouping labels, and rounded summary values.

| Check | R result | Python result | Match |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw row count | `nrow(nhanes)` = 105626 | `len(nhanes)` = 105626 | Yes |
| Column names | `names(nhanes)` = 18 columns | `nhanes.columns.tolist()` = 18 columns | Yes |
| Analysis rows after missingness filter | 87647 | 87647 | Yes |
| Group count | 6 grouped rows | 6 grouped rows | Yes |
| Summary values | `mean_bmi` and `sd_bmi` match after rounding | `mean_bmi` and `sd_bmi` match after rounding | Yes |

## Final note

The R and Python summaries agree on the number of filtered rows, the number of grouped rows, and the rounded BMI summary values after the same missing-data filtering and group definitions are applied. This confirms that the translated pandas analysis preserves the same analytic question and answer as the original R workflow.
